title: manchester like local 2026 09 05
text:
Moving back to Manchester after 15 years away felt like reuniting with an old friend who'd done well in life.
I grew up here in the 1980s and '90s and returned in 2022 to cover the north of England for Reuters after nearly two decades in London. The rain, homely pubs, music scene and dry sense of humour remain the same, but now skyscrapers tower over the city centre. While they're not to everyone's taste, I think they make Manchester feel grown-up and international — unlike the abandoned mills and grubby streets I knew as a kid.
Manchester has long been famous: it conjures the Industrial Revolution, suffragettes, Alan Turing, United and City, Oasis, and Daphne from "Frasier". Today, its renown has expanded to include world-class music venues, museums, great food, a vibrant nightlife and what claims to be Europe's largest gay village. Andy Burnham's rise from Greater Manchester mayor to British prime minister has put the city under a fresh spotlight: his launch of "Number 10 North," a new government base in the city centre, is meant as a counterweight to London's national economic and political dominance.
My friends say I picked the right time to be a journalist in Manchester, but really it's always been that way: people here are open and funny. That sparks conversation and the stories flow from there.
Here's how to experience the city like a Mancunian, or "Manc," as we'd say:
Getting around: In the city, buses and trams now run on a single "tap and go" system — the Bee Network — which you can pay for using a contactless card or phone. Local rail lines start joining the network from the end of 2026. Handy free buses also loop through the centre every few minutes, linking Piccadilly, Victoria and Deansgate train stations with the shops and museums.
But if you can, I recommend exploring Manchester on foot. The city centre is pretty compact and you can walk from one side to the other within half an hour.
Take in a gig: I have a side job as a musician and have played all over the world, so take it from me — Manchester punches above cities five times its size for live music. Many venues are repurposed buildings with long histories, sitting alongside the brand-new. The biggest and newest venue is Co-op Live, Britain's largest indoor arena, which has hosted Ed Sheeran, Lady Gaga and Bruce Springsteen since opening two years ago.
I prefer smaller venues though, and one of my favourites is New Century — a 1960s modernist ballroom with a disco-light ceiling, recently refitted into one of the best-sounding rooms in the city. In the hip Northern Quarter, you can find Band on the Wall, which ploughs its takings back into music lessons for local kids.
I have a particular soft spot for The Eagle Inn, an excellent pub in nearby Salford with a tiny live room attached.
It would be remiss not to mention the Hallé, Manchester's symphony orchestra and one of the oldest in the country. It plays at The Bridgewater Hall, one of the most acoustically perfect rooms in the world.
A good pint: When my local pub in south London turned into a sports bar, I knew it was time to come home. Manchester still has in abundance the comfy local boozers where the beer is good and chats spill over to the neighbouring table.
My local in Stockport, The Magnet — ranked by National Geographic Traveller as one of Britain's 12 best pubs — is one such place. Up the road, Ye Olde Vic is even cosier, but don't use foul language as you may get a ticking-off from the landlord.
In the city centre, Peveril of the Peak — "the Pev" to locals — is a picture-postcard with its 19th-century green tiling, although it fills up quickly with post-work drinkers. Cask has a wide selection of beers and friendly staff who will let you bring in your fish and chips from the takeaway across the road.
And be sure to head to The Castle Hotel in the Northern Quarter for a late-night drink around the jukebox.
Take in a match: Manchester is synonymous with football — or soccer, if you must.
Millions visit City's Etihad Stadium or United's Old Trafford every year. Match tickets are hard to get, but don't forget the smaller clubs. Salford City, Rochdale, Stockport County, Bury and even Macclesfield 15 miles (24 kilometres) to the south — my team — offer authentic experiences of English football at lower prices.
Rugby, both league and union, runs deep here too, and a trip to see Wigan Warriors or Sale Sharks makes for a great day out.
Culture fix: Manchester's museums lean into its history. The Science and Industry Museum tells the story of the city as a birthplace of the Industrial Revolution and modern computing and is great for kids, while the nearby People's History Museum charts the rise of democracy and workers' rights.
Two free art galleries are worth a couple of hours each: Manchester Art Gallery in the centre, with its fine Victorian art collection, and the Whitworth, whose glass-walled rooms open onto its own park out by the University of Manchester.
Over in Salford Quays, the Lowry houses the world's largest collection of work by LS Lowry, the painter of "matchstick men" who perhaps more than anyone captured the essence of northern England's industrial past.
Places to eat: I can't claim to have tried every fine-dining restaurant in Manchester, but the meal I had at the Michelin-starred Mana is probably the best of my life.
The Spärrows, under a railway arch, is difficult to describe — a sort of central European carb heaven — but I keep going back for the dumplings.
Interesting things are happening in my home turf of Stockport. The Royal Nawaab is an Indian and Pakistani banqueting venue based in a vast former office block shaped like a pyramid. It feels like something from a dream, but the food is tasty. And locals love the Mekong Cat, a little Southeast Asian noodle house which gets booked out fast. I recommend the Lao-style pho.
High-quality food halls have popped up across Greater Manchester over the last decade, making use of old market halls or industrial spaces, including Mackie Mayor in the Northern Quarter and Freight Island, next to the new Mayfield Park.
Unlike in London, excellent fish and chip shops are widespread.
Getting away: Liverpool is only 35 minutes away by train but a very different city — go for the grand waterfront, the Beatles heritage and a nightlife that rivals Manchester's. To the east, the Peak District National Park has rolling hills, dry-stone walls and pretty villages located less than an hour's drive from the city centre. On a sunny day, Manchester looks like a toy town from the top of Kinder Scout, the area's highest peak.
CITY MEMO DATA POINTS
Population: 3 million people
Price of a pint: Sub-£5 pints are still around, but getting rarer. Try a Pomona Island Factotum, a refreshing Manchester pale ale, at The Gas Lamp for about £5.60 ($7.60).
Price of fish and chips: £6.50 ($8.90) from Heaton Moor Fish Bar
Great place to see a sunset: Take a stroll around Salford Quays for a waterside view of the evening sky
Largest university: The University of Manchester, 46,000 students
($1 = 0.7393 pounds)
